title: Epsilon flow — small-payload inference sweep (scratch diary)
content:
Background / motivation:
- 'Epsilon flow' = high-rate, extremely small request payloads (user intent: single-token replies, short completions). These are common for edge chat UIs, token-limited assistants, and telemetry-derived prompts.
- Hypothesis: padding policies + cache priming have outsized effect on per-token cost and p99 latency. Small-payload workloads interact poorly with standard batching heuristics, causing either very high latency (long wait-for-batch) or low GPU utilization (tiny batches processed immediately).

Experiment goals:
1) Measure end-to-end latency distribution (p50/p95/p99) and throughput (QPS) for realistic epsilon flows.
2) Quantify trade-offs when applying different padding strategies (no-pad, pad-to-64, pad-to-256).
3) Compare model variants: fp16 vs int8/quantized (QAT-like profile) and observe jitter + KV cache effects.
4) Capture GPU occupancy and KV cache hit% per policy (warm vs cold).

Environment / setup:
- Platform: local Redwood Dedicated test pool (2xA100-equivalent per node).
- Serving runtime: runtime-v1.9.3 (branch: epsilon-batching-tweaks).
- Model: open-llama-7B adapted for inference; variants: fp16, 4bit-quant (LLM-Q4).
- Requests: fixed prompt base (~12 tokens prompt), expected generation: 1–6 tokens.
- Workload generator: synthetic client (python) that emits Poisson arrivals; peak offered QPS sweeps: [100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000] (per-node).
- Batcher settings: max_delay_ms default=5ms; max_batch_size default=64. Altered per run when noted.
- Padding policies tested:
  * no-pad (send actual token-length)
  * pad-64 (client pads all inputs to 64 tokens)
  * pad-256 (pad to 256)
- Cache: KV cache enabled; warm run = prefill with 10k similar prompts; cold run = empty cache.
- Observability: per-request latency, batch size at dispatch, queueing delay, GPU util (nvidia-smi), KV cache hit ratio, per-token compute ms.

Key measurements taken (aggregated per 10s window):
- qps_offered, qps_served, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, mean_batch_size, gpu_util_pct, kv_cache_hit_pct

Run summary (selected rows) — fp16 model, warm cache:
- Offered QPS 100:
  * no-pad: p50=6ms, p95=12ms, p99=20ms, mean_batch_size=3.2, gpu_util=18%, kv_hit=87%
  * pad-64: p50=9ms, p95=14ms, p99=25ms, mean_batch_size=8.1, gpu_util=34%, kv_hit=86%
  * pad-256: p50=14ms, p95=22ms, p99=40ms, mean_batch_size=15.6, gpu_util=49%, kv_hit=84%

- Offered QPS 1000:
  * no-pad: p50=9ms, p95=22ms, p99=65ms, mean_batch_size=7.9, gpu_util=61%, kv_hit=88%
  * pad-64: p50=11ms, p95=26ms, p99=72ms, mean_batch_size=28.7, gpu_util=82%, kv_hit=87%
  * pad-256: p50=19ms, p95=48ms, p99=130ms, mean_batch_size=63.0, gpu_util=94%, kv_hit=83%

Notes on fp16 warm-cache behavior:
- No-pad keeps per-request latency low at low QPS but at higher QPS p99 climbs due to microbursting and increased queueing variability. Mean batch size grows with QPS, but many tiny batches still go out (max_delay sometimes preempted).
- Pad-64 achieves a middle ground: consistent batching reduces per-token compute overhead but introduces base latency (padding cost + larger kernel runs). p95/p99 are smoother up to ~1k QPS.
- Pad-256 drives near-full GPU utilization at high QPS, but p99 suffers badly on tail due to queueing of oversized batches and longer kernel times, causing interference with lower-latency lanes.

Quantized (4bit) results, warm cache (selected):
- Offered QPS 1000, pad-64: p50=14ms, p95=32ms, p99=105ms, gpu_util=70%
- Observed that quantization reduces per-token compute time but increases variance: kernel bottoms out for tiny batches (vectorized paths less efficient), and memory layout yields longer cold-starts for specific kernels. Net effect: at medium QPS quantized variant often slightly worse tail.

Cold-cache runs (no prefill):
- Initial 30s period shows p99 spikes 2–3x as high across the board due to KV cache misses and model attention warmup. Pad policies don't mitigate this except by smoothing batch sizes.

Interesting micro-observations (logs):
- Several 1–2s spikes correlated with GC cycles in the runtime's slab allocator (runtime-v1.9.3). Need to follow up with a slot-size tuning patch (observed under pad-256, high batch churn).
- When max_delay_ms bumped to 10ms, mean batch size increases ~25% and p99 improves for pad-64 but p50 increases ~3–4ms. Trade-off acceptable for SLOs targeting p95.
- KV cache hit drop from 88% -> 81% between pad-64 and pad-256 at high QPS; likely because longer batches evict more slots and reduce effective sharing due to sequence-length variability.

Quick table (interpretation, not raw CSV):
- Latency-quality gradient: no-pad (lowest base latency, highest jitter) -> pad-64 (balanced) -> pad-256 (highest base latency, lowest jitter in some windows but worse worst-case).
- Cost-per-token: pad-256 lowest compute tokens per second for GPUs but increases overall p99 penalties and queuing artifacts that can worsen SLA violations — so cost savings are not automatically beneficial.

Actionable takeaways / next steps:
1) For epsilon flows, default to an adaptive pad-to-bucket policy: pad to nearest power-of-two bucket, capped at 64 tokens, unless explicit client opt-in for high-throughput (pad-256).
2) Implement dynamic max_delay: increase wait-for-batch when offered QPS crosses threshold (observed ~250 QPS per-core) to smooth p99 without blowing up p50. Empirically test 7–12ms window.
3) Investigate allocator GC spikes: add telemetry for slab churn and try patch that increases arena size when mean_batch_size>20.
4) Add a quick client-side option: 'latency_preference=low' to signal no-pad and shorter wait; 'throughput_preference=high' to encourage larger pads.
5) Re-run quantized kernels with kernel-fusion flags enabled (runtime branch) — early sign that quantized sparse paths need extra tuning.

Outstanding questions / experiments to schedule:
- How does real user prompt variation (not synthetic fixed prompt) change KV sharing patterns? Need a short replay test against production traces (anonymized).
- Evaluate pad-to-subtoken vs pad-to-token (tokenization changes padding distribution).
- Cost modeling: compute per-token cost delta when moving from no-pad -> pad-64 across different QPS slices (simulate monthly TCO).

Raw notes / log snippets (timestamps local):
- [2025-08-03 09:02] run-start: 1k QPS pad-64 fp16 warm; observed batch-size heartbeat ~28–32; occasional 1.5s tail spike at 09:02:44; correlates with slab GC.
- [2025-08-03 09:27] increased max_delay_ms to 10ms; p99 dropped from ~72ms -> ~46ms for pad-64 at 1k QPS. p50 rose ~2ms.
- [2025-08-03 10:15] quantized pad-256 run: GPU util -> 96%; p99=130ms; but cost-per-token projection down 18% if tail controlled.

Immediate TODO (who/when):
- @Arjun: add slab allocator telemetry + link to runtime PR (by 2025-08-15).
- @Sasha: schedule replay job on anonymized trace subset (by 2025-08-12).
- @me (Morgan): prototype adaptive pad-to-bucket in client shim and test with 250/500/1k QPS (by 2025-08-18).

One-line summary for Slack/standup:
- Epsilon flow experiments show pad-to-64 + small increase in max_delay gives best p95/p99 stabilization for mixed small-payload workloads; pad-256 wastes latency SLOs despite higher GPU efficiency. Next: adaptive padding + allocator telemetry.

Free-form scratch (ideas):
- Could we add a tiny in-proxy microcache (1–2ms lookup) for exact repeated short prompts to reduce KV misses? Risk: added hop, but might pay off for very high cache-hit fractions.
- Explore tiny model ensembling: use ultra-fast distilled 350M for 1-token replies and fallback to main model only on longer turns. This would change routing but may reduce overall cost.

End of diary entry.
